Brotherhood Covenant
BRUH-ther-hood KUH-vuh-nuhnt
proper noun
The covenant bond of brotherly love among the members of Christ’s church; from the biblical “brotherhood” and the covenant of mutual love and watchfulness.

📖 Biblical Definition

The brotherhood covenant is the bond of brotherly love and mutual duty that joins the members of Christ’s church one to another—the covenant, whether formally written or simply lived, by which believers commit to love, watch over, bear with, and build up one another as brethren. Scripture names the church a brotherhood and commands its love: love the brotherhood; let brotherly love continue. The Lord gave it as His new commandment: that ye love one another, as I have loved you, that ye also love one another—and by this all men shall know we are His disciples. The psalmist sang its sweetness: behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Many churches express this bond in a church covenant—a solemn agreement of members to walk together in love, to watch over one another, to attend the worship and ordinances, to submit to discipline, and to seek one another’s good—giving formal shape to the mutual obligations the New Testament everywhere assumes. The dictionary reads the brotherhood covenant as the committed, covenantal love of church members for one another: not a loose and optional friendliness, but a binding fellowship of brethren who have given themselves to the Lord and to one another, to love, watch over, and build up the body in unity, until they dwell together for ever in the household of God.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The covenant bond of brotherly love and mutual duty joining the members of Christ’s church; committed, watchful love—often formalized in a church covenant—not a loose friendliness.

Heb 13:1 — "Let brotherly love continue."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Church membership is reduced to a loose, optional friendliness with no real bond or accountability; the brotherhood covenant is the committed, watchful love the New Testament assumes among brethren.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The drift to name is the reduction of church fellowship to a loose, consumer-style friendliness—believers attending when convenient, committing to no one, accountable to no one, treating the church as a service to be sampled rather than a brotherhood to be joined. In this drift the rich New Testament language of loving the brotherhood and watching over one another is hollowed out, and the church becomes a crowd of strangers who happen to share a building. But the Scripture knows no such uncommitted Christianity; it everywhere assumes a real, binding fellowship of brethren who belong to one another in the Lord.

The principle to recover is the committed, covenantal love of church members. The brotherhood is to be loved, brotherly love to continue, the new commandment kept—that we love one another as Christ loved us; and how good and pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity. Many churches give this formal shape in a church covenant, a solemn mutual agreement to walk together in love, to watch over one another, to attend the worship and ordinances, and to submit to loving discipline. Whether written or lived, the bond is real: brethren who have given themselves to the Lord and to one another, to love, bear with, and build up the body, until they dwell together for ever in the family of God.
